title: The Message of Acts & Baptism and Fullness
author: stott

entries.title: The Spirit and the Worldwide Witness: Acts 1:8 as the Programme of the Church
entries.content_summary: Stott takes Acts 1:8 as the key that unlocks the whole book. The apostles' question about restoring the kingdom to Israel is redirected: they are not to speculate about dates or a nationalist kingdom but to receive power from the Holy Spirit and become witnesses. The verse is at once a promise and a table of contents -- 'Jerusalem, all Judea and Samaria, and the ends of the earth' maps the very expansion Luke will narrate. Stott underlines that the Spirit is given primarily for mission, not private enrichment: the power promised is power to witness to Christ. The church is thus, by definition, a Spirit-empowered missionary community, and the same commission still defines its task. Pentecost, when it comes, will be the equipping for exactly this worldwide testimony.
entries.content_detail:
Stott gives Acts 1:8 a pivotal place, calling it in effect the text of which the rest of Acts is the exposition. The setting is the risen Christ's final conversation with the apostles, and it opens with their question about whether he will now 'restore the kingdom to Israel' (1:6). Stott reads Jesus' reply as a gentle but firm correction of three assumptions embedded in that question. Their preoccupation with the timing of the end is set aside: it is not for them to know 'times or seasons.' Their nationalist and political conception of the kingdom is quietly redirected toward a spiritual, worldwide reign advanced by witness. And their passivity as mere spectators of a restored Israel is replaced by an active commission.

The positive content is the promise of power and the definition of a task. 'You will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you.' Stott is careful about the purpose of this power: it is not primarily for personal ecstasy, moral transformation, or private blessing, but for witness -- 'you will be my witnesses.' The Spirit and mission are bound together; the church receives the Spirit in order to testify to Christ.

Stott also reads the geography of the verse as the deliberate outline of the book. The gospel will move out in widening circles: 'in Jerusalem' (chapters 1-7), 'in all Judea and Samaria' (chapters 8-12), and 'to the end of the earth' (chapters 13-28), reaching at last to Rome, the empire's centre. The programme is centrifugal and universal, breaking every barrier of race and region.

From this Stott draws his large thesis about Acts and about the church: the people of God are essentially a missionary people, constituted and empowered by the Spirit for the task of world evangelization. The command was given to the apostles first, but Stott insists the underlying mandate continues; the church that stops witnessing has forgotten why the Spirit was given. Pentecost, narrated in the next chapter, is precisely the fulfilment of this promise -- the equipping of the church for its worldwide witness.

entries.title: Pentecost: The Spirit Poured Out and the Last Days Begun
entries.content_summary: Stott presents Pentecost as a unique, unrepeatable event in salvation history, comparable to the incarnation and resurrection: the once-for-all inauguration of the age of the Spirit. When the disciples are 'filled with the Holy Spirit' and speak in other tongues (2:4), the many languages are a sign that the gospel is for every nation -- a reversal of Babel's scattering. In his sermon Peter interprets the outpouring by Joel: this is the promised deluge of the Spirit 'in the last days,' now poured out not on a chosen few but on all flesh -- sons and daughters, young and old, slave and free (2:17). Stott thus reads Pentecost christologically and eschatologically: the exalted Jesus has poured out the Spirit, and the new age has dawned, though the event itself belongs to the foundation of the church, not to normal repeated experience.
entries.content_detail:
Stott interprets the day of Pentecost as a landmark event in the history of salvation, and he insists on its uniqueness. Just as the incarnation and the resurrection happened once and cannot be repeated, so Pentecost was the once-for-all inauguration of the era of the Spirit -- the moment the ascended Christ poured out on his church the Spirit he had promised. The dramatic phenomena, the sound like a rushing wind and the tongues as of fire, are signs marking this decisive beginning.

Of the speaking 'in other tongues' (2:4), Stott takes the plain sense of the narrative: the disciples spoke real, recognizable human languages, so that the international crowd each heard the mighty works of God in their own tongue. He draws out the theological symbolism: whereas at Babel human languages were confused and the nations scattered, at Pentecost the language barrier is momentarily overcome, signalling that the gospel is for all peoples and that God is gathering a worldwide church. The gift is a sign of the universality of the good news.

The heart of Stott's exposition is Peter's interpretation of the event through the prophecy of Joel (2:16-21). Peter declares, 'this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel' -- the promised outpouring of the Spirit 'in the last days.' Stott stresses two things about this. First, the phrase 'the last days' means the new age has actually begun; the church lives in the era of fulfilment inaugurated by the Spirit's coming. Second, the outpouring is strikingly democratic and universal: no longer reserved for prophets, priests, and kings, the Spirit now comes upon 'all flesh' -- sons and daughters, young and old, male and female, slave and free (2:17-18). What in the Old Testament was occasional and selective becomes, in the new age, the common possession of the whole people of God.

Stott also notes the christological climax of Peter's sermon: it is the crucified, risen, and exalted Jesus who, having received the Spirit from the Father, has 'poured out this that you yourselves see and hear' (2:33). Pentecost is thus Christ's own act. For Stott it stands as the foundational, non-repeatable birth of the Spirit-filled church, even as the fullness it inaugurates remains the church's continuing possession.

entries.title: Repent, Be Baptized, Receive the Spirit: The Norm of Christian Initiation
entries.chapter_or_episode: Acts 2:37-39 -- Peter's answer to the crowd
entries.content_summary: When the convicted crowd asks what to do, Peter's reply (2:38) gives Stott the normal pattern of Christian beginnings: repentance and faith, expressed in baptism, issuing in the forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Holy Spirit. Crucially, Stott insists these belong together as facets of one initiation, not as a first and then a separate, later second blessing. The gift of the Spirit is promised to every penitent believer, not to a spiritual elite. And the promise is expansive: 'for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself' (2:39) -- reaching across generations and, Stott notes, already hinting at the Gentiles. This text, not the exceptional cases later in Acts, is Stott's baseline for what conversion normally includes.
entries.content_detail:
For Stott, Peter's answer to the Pentecost crowd is the theological centre of gravity for the doctrine of Christian initiation, and he returns to it repeatedly. Cut to the heart, the hearers ask, 'What shall we do?' Peter replies, 'Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit' (2:38). Stott reads this as setting out the normal ingredients of becoming a Christian, bound together as parts of one whole rather than strung out as separate stages. Repentance and the faith it implies are the inward turning; baptism is its outward expression and seal; forgiveness of sins is the blessing received; and the gift of the Holy Spirit is the crowning endowment. All four belong to Christian beginnings.

Stott makes two points he regards as decisive against a 'second-blessing' theology. First, the gift of the Spirit here is promised to all who repent and are baptized, not to a special class of Christians who go on to some further experience. It is the birthright of every believer, integral to conversion-initiation itself. Second, there is no interval or second condition interposed between believing and receiving the Spirit; the Spirit is part of the initial package, not a later supplement to be sought by those already converted.

The reach of the promise is, for Stott, equally striking. 'The promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself' (2:39). Stott notes the widening scope: it spans generations ('your children'), and it extends to 'all who are far off' -- a phrase that, in the light of the rest of Acts, already anticipates the inclusion of the Gentiles. And the whole rests on divine initiative: it is granted to 'everyone whom the Lord our God calls,' so that the gift is grounded in God's own summoning grace, not in human attainment.

Stott therefore treats Acts 2:38-39, rather than the irregular episodes that follow in Samaria, Caesarea, and Ephesus, as the norm. Those later cases are, in his reading, exceptional and transitional; this is the pattern -- repentance, baptism, forgiveness, and the gift of the Spirit received together by everyone God calls.

entries.title: The Samaritan Delay: Why the Spirit Came Through the Apostles
entries.chapter_or_episode: Acts 8:14-17 -- the Spirit and the Samaritans
entries.content_summary: The Samaritan believers present the famous anomaly: they believe Philip's preaching and are baptized, yet the Spirit does not fall on them until Peter and John come down and lay hands on them (8:15-17). Stott resists using this as a proof text for a routine two-stage Christian experience. He reads it instead as a deliberate, exceptional act of God suited to a unique moment in the mission's advance. Given the old, bitter Jew-Samaritan schism, God withheld the Spirit until the Jerusalem apostles could be present, so that the birth of the Samaritan church would be visibly one with the mother church and no rival, schismatic Christianity could arise. The delay, Stott argues, concerns church unity at a hinge point in Acts, not a template requiring every believer to seek the Spirit as a distinct second step.
entries.content_detail:
The conversion of the Samaritans in Acts 8 poses what Stott frankly acknowledges is a genuine difficulty for any tidy doctrine of initiation. Philip preaches Christ in Samaria; the people believe and are baptized; and yet, unusually, the Holy Spirit does not come upon them at that point. Only when the apostles Peter and John travel down from Jerusalem, pray, and lay hands on them do the Samaritans receive the Spirit (8:15-17). The narrative openly notes that 'the Spirit had not yet fallen on any of them' (8:16).

Stott's chief concern is to interpret this rightly rather than to let it overturn the norm of Acts 2:38. He rejects the use of the episode as a proof text for the doctrine that Spirit-reception is normally a distinct second stage following conversion. Two features tell against generalizing from it: it is presented as an exception, precisely because it is out of the ordinary; and it belongs to a strategic moment in the geographical advance charted in Acts 1:8, the gospel's first crossing of a major ethnic boundary from Jews to Samaritans.

The explanation Stott favours turns on the long and bitter hostility between Jews and Samaritans. Had the Samaritan believers received the Spirit independently, through Philip alone and apart from the Jerusalem apostles, there was a real danger that a separate, rival Samaritan church would spring up, perpetuating the old schism inside the body of Christ. So, on Stott's reading, God sovereignly delayed the gift until the leaders of the mother church could be present, lay on hands, and thereby visibly incorporate the new Samaritan believers into the one apostolic church. The withholding served the unity of the church at a decisive turning point; it demonstrated that there is one people of God, not two.

The strange episode with Simon the sorcerer, who tries to buy the power to confer the Spirit (8:18-24), fits this reading: it shows how easily spiritual gifts could be misunderstood and abused, and it underscores that the Spirit is God's gift, not a commodity. For Stott, then, Acts 8 is a transitional, unrepeatable event about the unity of the expanding church, not a paradigm requiring ordinary Christians to pursue a second blessing after conversion.

entries.title: The Gentile Pentecost: The Spirit Falls at Cornelius' House
entries.chapter_or_episode: Acts 10:44-48 -- the Spirit poured out on the Gentiles
entries.content_summary: At Cornelius' house the Spirit interrupts Peter mid-sermon and falls on the Gentile listeners (10:44), and the circumcised believers who came with him are 'astonished' that the gift is poured out even on Gentiles (10:45). Stott calls this the Gentile Pentecost: God's own dramatic verdict that the uncircumcised are accepted on precisely the same terms as Jews. The sequence is striking -- the Spirit comes before baptism and without any laying on of hands -- because God is settling a disputed question by sovereign action, overturning Peter's inherited scruples and pre-empting any demand that Gentiles first become Jews. For Stott the point is not a paradigm of how individuals today receive the Spirit, but a turning point in redemptive history: the door of faith is thrown open to the nations, and the church must recognize what God has done.
entries.content_detail:
Stott regards the Cornelius episode as one of the great watersheds of Acts, the moment the gospel decisively breaks the barrier between Jew and Gentile. The build-up is elaborate and deliberate: the double vision given to Cornelius and to Peter, Peter's rooftop lesson that he must call no person common or unclean, and his arrival at a Gentile household with the confession that 'God shows no partiality' (10:34). All of this prepares for the climactic act.

While Peter is still preaching, before he can even finish, 'the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word' (10:44). Stott highlights the reaction of 'the believers from among the circumcised' who had come with Peter: they were 'amazed' -- astonished, even scandalized -- that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out 'even on the Gentiles' (10:45), for they heard them speaking in tongues and extolling God, just as had happened at the original Pentecost. Stott stresses this parallel, which is why he calls the event a 'Gentile Pentecost': God gave to these uncircumcised believers the identical gift he had given to the Jewish disciples at the beginning.

The order of events is, for Stott, the theological heart of the passage. The Spirit is given before baptism and without the laying on of hands -- an order different again from both Acts 2 and Acts 8. Stott's explanation is that God deliberately took the initiative out of human hands to settle a contested question by his own unmistakable action. By pouring out the Spirit on Gentiles as Gentiles, before any ritual and without their first becoming Jews, God demonstrated that he accepts them on exactly the same terms as Jewish believers -- by grace, through faith. This overturned Peter's own deep-seated scruples and left him only one conclusion: 'Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?' (10:47).

Stott notes that Peter later appeals to precisely this event to justify himself in Jerusalem, arguing that since 'God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us' (11:17), it was not for him to stand in God's way. So for Stott the episode is not a template for individual Spirit-reception today, with its unusual sequence, but a unique, epoch-making act in redemptive history: God himself flinging open the door of faith to the nations, and the church learning to recognize and accept what God has done.

entries.title: The Ephesian Twelve: Disciples of John Brought Up to Date
entries.content_summary: Paul finds about twelve 'disciples' at Ephesus and asks whether they received the Spirit when they believed (19:2); they have not so much as heard that there is a Holy Spirit, and prove to know only John's baptism. Stott argues they were not yet Christians in the full new-covenant sense at all, but followers of John the Baptist stranded before Pentecost -- believers in the promise who had never received its fulfilment. Paul instructs them, baptizes them into the name of Jesus, lays hands on them, and the Spirit comes with tongues and prophecy (19:6). Stott therefore denies this supports a two-stage doctrine for ordinary Christians; it is the unique case of pre-Christian disciples being completed, their deficient initiation made good, so that they pass from Old-Covenant anticipation into full Christian faith and the gift of the Spirit.
entries.content_detail:
The dozen 'disciples' Paul meets at Ephesus (Acts 19:1-7) are, for Stott, another case regularly pressed into service for a second-blessing theology, and again he argues the text will not bear that weight. Paul's opening question, 'Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?' (19:2), is sometimes read as though it distinguished receiving the Spirit from believing, as two separate steps. Stott counters that the more natural sense is coincident: did you receive the Spirit when (that is, at the point at which) you believed? The question expects that faith and the Spirit belong together, and Paul asks it precisely because something about these men seemed defective.

The defect quickly emerges. They reply that they have not even heard 'that there is a Holy Spirit,' and under questioning it appears they had received only 'John's baptism' (19:3). Stott concludes that they were not Christians in the full sense at all. They were, at best, disciples of John the Baptist -- people who had responded to John's call to repentance and his announcement of the coming One, but who had never come through into the new-covenant reality inaugurated at Pentecost. They stood, spiritually, on the far side of the great divide, holding to the promise without its fulfilment. The word 'disciples' here, Stott notes, need not mean Christian disciples; it describes their attachment to John.

Paul's response confirms this diagnosis. He does not treat them as believers seeking a second blessing; he completes their deficient initiation. He explains that John's was a baptism of repentance pointing forward to Jesus; on hearing this, they are baptized 'in the name of the Lord Jesus' -- Christian baptism proper -- and when Paul lays his hands on them, the Holy Spirit comes upon them and they speak in tongues and prophesy (19:5-6). In other words, they are brought at last from Old-Covenant anticipation into full Christian experience.

For Stott the lesson is the opposite of the two-stage reading. This is not a Christian's later reception of the Spirit; it is the belated, once-only regularizing of men who had never been properly Christian at all. Like the other 'irregular' episodes in Acts, it is transitional and exceptional, and it leaves untouched the norm of Acts 2:38, in which repentance, baptism, and the gift of the Spirit belong together at the very outset.

entries.title: One Baptism, Many Fillings: Spirit-Baptism as Initiation, Fullness as the Norm
entries.content_summary: This cell states the central thesis of Stott's Baptism and Fullness. The 'baptism of the Spirit,' he argues, is not a second blessing for advanced Christians but the initial gift bestowed on every believer at conversion -- the one act by which, as Paul says, 'we were all baptized into one body' (1Co.12.13). It is therefore universal among Christians and, in that sense, unrepeatable. What Scripture then commands repeatedly is something different: 'be filled with the Spirit' (Eph.5.18), a present-tense, continuous imperative addressed to all. Stott's conclusion reframes the whole Pentecostal debate: the New Testament norm is not to seek a subsequent baptism one may still lack, but to go on being filled with the Spirit one has already received. Fullness, not a second baptism, is the abiding call, and it may be enjoyed and renewed many times.
entries.content_detail:
This entry gathers the constructive argument of Stott's book Baptism and Fullness, which sets out to distinguish two things the popular teaching of a 'second blessing' had run together. Stott's central contention is a careful separation of terms: the baptism of the Spirit on one hand, and the fullness of the Spirit on the other.

Regarding the baptism of the Spirit, Stott argues from the New Testament usage that it is initiatory and universal, not a later, higher experience reserved for some Christians. His decisive text is 1 Corinthians 12:13: 'in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body.' He stresses every part of it. It is 'all' -- so Spirit-baptism is the common possession of every believer, not the privilege of an elite; the Corinthians, whom Paul is rebuking for their immaturity, are included. It is past tense, 'we were baptized' -- so it is something already true of them, tied to their conversion and incorporation into Christ's body, not a blessing still to be sought. On this reading, Spirit-baptism is simply another way of describing entry into new life in Christ; and if a person is in Christ at all, that person has the Spirit (Romans 8:9). It is therefore, like conversion, unrepeatable.

Regarding the fullness of the Spirit, Stott points to a different and repeated note in the New Testament. The great command is Ephesians 5:18: 'be filled with the Spirit.' He draws attention to the grammar. The verb is a plural imperative addressed to all Christians, so it is a command, not merely a privilege for the few. It is passive, 'be filled' -- fullness is God's work, to be received, not self-generated. And it is present continuous in force -- 'go on being filled' -- describing not a single crisis but an ongoing, renewable condition. Where baptism is once-for-all, filling is meant to be repeated and habitual; a Christian may be filled, and filled again.

Stott's pastoral conclusion reframes the whole 'second blessing' debate. The mistake, he argues, is to make baptism the ongoing quest and to divide the church into the Spirit-baptized 'haves' and the un-baptized 'have-nots.' The New Testament pattern is the reverse: the baptism is presupposed as belonging to all believers already, while the filling is the perpetual command and the proper ambition. Christians are not to seek a second baptism they supposedly lack, but continually to be filled with the Spirit they have received -- fullness, not a further baptism, being the abiding norm of the Christian life.

entries.title: The Fruit of the Spirit: Christlike Character as the Primary Evidence
entries.content_summary: For Stott the true and primary evidence of the Spirit's fullness is not spectacular gifts but Christlike character -- the fruit of the Spirit (Gal.5.22). Paul sets this ninefold fruit against the works of the flesh, and Stott notes that it is singular ('fruit,' not 'fruits'): a single cluster of graces, headed by love, that the Spirit grows in everyone he indwells. Gifts can be counterfeited and can coexist with immaturity, but the fruit cannot be faked; it is the Spirit reproducing the likeness of Jesus. So when people ask how to tell whether someone is filled with the Spirit, Stott points not to tongues or ecstasy but to love, joy, peace, and self-control. This keeps the doctrine of the Spirit tethered to sanctification and to the imitation of Christ, guarding it against a merely sensational spirituality.
entries.content_detail:
Having argued that fullness is the true norm of Spirit-filled living, Stott turns to the question of evidence: how is the fullness of the Spirit actually recognized? Much popular teaching answered by pointing to the more dramatic gifts, above all speaking in tongues, as the decisive sign. Stott's reply, developed in Baptism and Fullness, is to relocate the primary evidence from gifts to fruit, and his key text is Galatians 5:22-23.

Paul there contrasts two harvests. On one side stand 'the works of the flesh' -- a list of sins of sex, religion, society, and drink that betray unregenerate human nature. On the other stands 'the fruit of the Spirit': love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control. Stott makes a grammatical observation he regards as significant: Paul speaks of 'fruit' in the singular, not 'fruits.' The nine graces are not a menu from which the Spirit-filled select a few, but a single ripening cluster, an organic whole that the Spirit grows together in the believer -- and it is headed, deliberately, by love, which for Stott (as in 1 Corinthians 13) is the supreme and comprehensive Christian grace.

The force of preferring fruit to gifts, Stott argues, lies in what each can and cannot prove. Spiritual gifts, including tongues, can be counterfeited or imitated, and, as the Corinthian church painfully showed, they can coexist with carnality, jealousy, and immaturity; a person may be highly gifted and yet spiritually shallow. The fruit of the Spirit cannot be faked in the same way, because it is nothing less than the character of Christ himself being reproduced in the disciple. Love, joy, peace, and self-control are the Spirit's own likeness formed within, and they grow only where the Spirit is genuinely at work.

Stott's conclusion is therefore both a corrective and a pastoral reassurance. When someone asks how to tell whether a person -- or oneself -- is filled with the Spirit, the answer is not to look first for the sensational but to look for Christlikeness: is love growing? Is there joy, patience, gentleness, self-mastery? By tying the evidence of the Spirit's fullness to sanctification and the imitation of Christ, Stott guards the doctrine against a spirituality that prizes experience and power over holiness, and he restores the fruit of the Spirit to its place as the surest mark that the Spirit is filling a life.
